strengths: Tackles an exceptionally challenging and under-explored problem: high-frequency 3D dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis of real flames under extremely sparse (three-camera) view constraints.

Clever, practical hardware-software co-design: The use of an ESP32 microcontroller with an LED Gray code and rolling shutter strip patterns to achieve sub-frame (~15 µs) synchronization across consumer cameras operating at 400 Hz is elegant and reproducible.

Well-motivated reconstruction pipeline: Decoupling the static background (via temporal minimum intensity projection and stereo-monocular depth fusion) from the dynamic fire, coupled with SVD-based multi-view optical flow projection into a 3D velocity field, provides robust initialization that prevents geometric collapse in sparse-view settings.

Valuable real-world dataset comprising 17 distinct sequences spanning various fuel types (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper) and backgrounds, which will benefit the dynamic reconstruction and graphics communities.

Convincing qualitative and quantitative results in dynamic regions: Outperforms standard 4D Gaussian Splatting baselines significantly in PSNR/SSIM on the flame regions and avoids the severe spatial degradation seen in unregularized baselines.
weaknesses: Evaluation setup lacks quantitative held-out novel view synthesis: The quantitative evaluation splits frames temporally (every 8th frame), meaning the test views share the same camera viewpoints as training. For a 3-camera setup claiming 3D reconstruction, holding out one camera view (or adding a 4th reference camera for evaluation) would be much more indicative of true geometric and multi-view consistency than temporal interpolation alone.

Limited comparative baselines: The paper only compares against two general 4DGS methods (Wu et al. and Yang et al.). It does not benchmark against FreeTimeGS directly without the flow initialization or against prior methods targeting semi-transparent/volumetric dynamic phenomena.

The necessity of the rolling-shutter model is questionable: In the ablation table (Table 2), removing the rolling shutter modeling ('GlobalShutter') yields almost identical metrics (PSNRflame 27.48 vs. 27.46; RMSEdepth 0.0408 vs. 0.0412), suggesting that at 400 Hz, rolling shutter distortions have negligible impact on the reconstruction.

Representation limitations: Adopting a linear velocity per Gaussian within FreeTimeGS limits the ability to model complex, turbulent, and vortical flame structures over longer horizons, which can lead to temporal oversmoothing as acknowledged in the limitations.

strengths: Addresses a very challenging and under-explored problem: high-frequency 3D reconstruction of transparent, highly turbulent, and emissive phenomena (fire) from an extremely sparse camera setup (only three views).

Presents an effective and elegant multi-stage pipeline: decoupling static and dynamic scene components, fusing 2D optical flows into a regularized 3D voxel motion field, and using this field to initialize dynamic Gaussians with temporal lifetimes and linear velocities.

Clever and practical hardware-software co-design: the authors construct an inexpensive synchronization system utilizing an ESP32, Gray-coded LEDs, and CMOS rolling-shutter readout characteristics to achieve ~15 microsecond-level synchronization across unsynchronized commodity high-speed cameras.

Introduces and releases a diverse real-world high-speed dataset comprising 17 video sequences across varying fuels (propane, wood, cardboard, paper, gasoline) captured at 400 Hz, which will be a valuable asset to the dynamic reconstruction community.

Quantitative and qualitative results convincingly demonstrate that the proposed method avoids the severe spatial degeneration and overfitting observed in existing 4D Gaussian Splatting baselines under extreme sparse-view conditions.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation splits data temporally (holding out every 8th frame) rather than spatially (holding out an unseen camera viewpoint). While using only three cameras makes spatial holdouts difficult, including a fourth held-out view for at least a subset of scenes would provide much stronger evidence for the quality of novel view synthesis in 3D.

The evaluation of 3D geometry relies on monocular depth estimation (DepthAnythingV2) as a pseudo-ground-truth proxy (RSMEdepth). Because monocular depth estimators typically fail or produce artifacts on semi-transparent, emissive media like flames (as acknowledged in Fig. 9), quantitative geometric conclusions must be taken with caution.

The modeled rolling-shutter compensation shows minimal to no quantitative impact in the ablation experiments (Table 2: PSNRflame 27.46 for Baseline vs. 27.48 for GlobalShutter), suggesting that this component may not be essential at the current capture resolution and shutter speed, despite being claimed as a contribution.

The assumption of linear velocity per Gaussian within FreeTimeGS restricts the representation to high frame rates (400 Hz) and short Gaussian lifespans, leaving complex non-linear turbulence and long-range coherent tracking for future work.

strengths: Tackles an inherently challenging and under-explored domain in 4D dynamic reconstruction: modeling semi-transparent, emissive, and highly volatile phenomena (flames) under extreme sparse-view conditions (only three cameras).

Clever and practical hardware engineering: The authors design an affordable synchronization rig using an ESP32 microcontroller with Gray-code frame counters and LED strips that leverage rolling shutter readout patterns to achieve microsecond-scale sub-frame temporal alignment across consumer GoPros at 400 fps.

Collects an interesting and diverse real-world fire dataset spanning 17 scenes across various fuel types (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper), which will be a useful resource for dynamic scene modeling.

The pipeline demonstrates plausible temporal continuity and visual quality on difficult fire dynamics by decoupling static background modeling from dynamic flame regions initialized via 3D projected optical flow.
weaknesses: Flawed evaluation protocol for novel view synthesis: The quantitative evaluation splits data purely temporally (holding out every 8th frame while training on all three camera views). For a 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis method, evaluating held-out spatial camera viewpoints is critical to prove the method learns true 3D volumetric structure rather than interpolating along the known three camera poses.

Problematic depth evaluation: The authors evaluate rendered depth accuracy (RMSEdepth) against Depth Anything V2 monocular depth maps. Monocular depth models are trained on rigid/diffuse surfaces and fundamentally struggle with transparent, emissive flames (as the authors themselves acknowledge in Fig. 9). Benchmarking against an unreliable pseudo-ground-truth undermines the validity of the reported depth scores.

Minimal impact from rolling-shutter modeling: The ablation study (Table 2) demonstrates that disabling rolling-shutter compensation (GlobalShutter) yields virtually identical numerical results (PSNR_flame 27.48 vs 27.46, SSIM_flame 0.8472 vs 0.8469, RMSE_depth 0.0408 vs 0.0412). Given that rolling shutter is presented as a primary technical contribution, the lack of measurable quantitative benefit at 400 Hz capture weakens this claim.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The framework largely integrates existing tools without substantial representation innovation: standard PatchMatch Stereo and Depth Anything V2 for static depth, MEMFOF for 2D flow, standard linear back-projection/Tikhonov regularization for 3D flow, and the FreeTimeGS primitive parameterization (lifetime and linear velocity) for rendering.

Missing comparisons with relevant sparse-view dynamic baselines: The comparison is restricted to standard dense-view 4DGS baselines (Wu et al. and Yang et al.), which are not tailored for sparse-camera capture. Comparisons against flow-guided or sparse-view dynamic neural radiance/splatting formulations (e.g., DynIBaR, MoSca, or FreeTimeGS with depth priors) are absent.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored and notoriously difficult problem: sparse-view 4D reconstruction of transient, emissive, and non-rigid volumetric phenomena (fire) where conventional dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods fail due to assumptions of surface persistence and smooth deformation.

The technical design is well-motivated and cohesive: combining temporal minimum intensity projection and stereo-monocular depth fusion for static background decoupling, followed by a 3D voxel flow initialization derived from regularized multi-view 2D optical flow to bootstrap transient flame Gaussians.

Presents an impressive engineering effort with a custom ESP32-based visual synchronization setup leveraging rolling-shutter effects to achieve ~15 µs temporal alignment across high-speed (400 Hz) commodity cameras.

Introduces both an extensive real-world high-speed dataset across diverse fuel types and a synthetic Mantaflow benchmark with a novel density-weighted volumetric evaluation protocol (DVE) for measuring physical velocity fidelity.

Strong experimental results and comprehensive ablations demonstrating clear qualitative and quantitative advantages over state-of-the-art dynamic GS baselines (4DGS, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) in appearance, depth consistency, and motion plausibility.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation on the real-world dataset is performed primarily on temporally held-out frames (every 8th frame) rather than on a held-out camera viewpoint. Given that sparse-view novel view synthesis is a primary motivation, quantitative validation on a held-out spatial viewpoint (e.g., training on 2 cameras and testing on 1, or adding a 4th held-out camera) would make the novel view synthesis claims much stronger.

The reconstruction pipeline is heavily sequential and dependent on multiple external heuristics/models (temporal min-projection for background separation, DepthAnythingV2, MEMFOF optical flow, COLMAP PatchMatchStereo). As noted in the discussion, optical flow estimation on turbulent, semi-transparent fire is inherently noisy, and errors can propagate directly into the 3D velocity initialization.
The motion representation assumes local constant linear velocity over each Gaussian's temporal lifespan, which can oversmooth fine-scale turbulent eddies and non-linear vortical combustion dynamics.
Minor formatting oversight: Section I in the Supplementary Material omits the URL placeholder ('at').

strengths: Addresses an ambitious and notoriously difficult problem: 3D reconstruction and dynamic novel-view synthesis of volumetric, emissive, and highly volatile phenomena (fire) under extreme view sparsity (only three cameras).

Presents a coherent and well-motivated pipeline that combines static-dynamic separation (via temporal minimum intensity projection and monocular-stereo depth alignment), a closed-form multi-view 2D optical flow fusion into a 3D voxelized motion field, and transient Gaussian splatting.

Proposes an ingenious, low-cost visual synchronization solution using an ESP32 and rolling-shutter CMOS exploitation to achieve sub-frame (~15 µs) temporal alignment across consumer high-speed cameras.

Introduces a sensible velocity evaluation protocol (Density-weighted Volumetric Evaluation, DVE) evaluated on synthetic Mantaflow fire simulations, along with an extensive real-world dataset comprising 17 high-speed (400 Hz) multi-view fire sequences across diverse fuel types.

Clear qualitative and quantitative superiority over dynamic Gaussian Splatting baselines (4DGS, FreeTimeGS, Grid4D), effectively overcoming common failure modes such as geometric absorption and depth collapse.
weaknesses: The core dynamic Gaussian representation (temporal Gaussian opacity envelope and constant linear velocity) is largely adapted from FreeTimeGS, making the algorithmic novelty somewhat incremental as a combination of existing tools (MEMFOF flow, DepthAnythingV2, PatchMatch, FreeTimeGS formulation).

The linear velocity model over Gaussian lifespans is a strong simplifying assumption that struggles to capture complex turbulent eddies and buoyancy acceleration in real fire, as acknowledged in the limitations.

The experimental validation in Table 1 evaluates held-out time frames (temporal interpolation) rather than held-out viewpoints (spatial novel view synthesis). While novel-view trajectories are shown qualitatively, quantitative evaluation on a held-out camera view would provide stronger evidence of true 3D spatial fidelity under sparse coverage.

Reliance on 2D optical flow (MEMFOF) on flame regions can be brittle due to severe brightness constancy violations, transparent flame layers, and non-rigid appearance changes, potentially propagating errors into the 3D initial velocity field.

strengths: Addresses a distinct and challenging problem: sparse-view (3 cameras) dynamic reconstruction of flames, an emissive and non-rigid volumetric phenomenon where standard dynamic Gaussian Splatting formulations suffer from geometric absorption and depth collapse.

Well-designed, lightweight reconstruction framework: cleanly decouples static background (using stereo and monocular depth priors) from dynamic fire, modeling the latter as transient Gaussians initialized from a fused 3D optical flow field.

Clever and practical hardware capture setup: achieves microsecond-level visual temporal synchronization across consumer high-speed cameras (GoPro at 400 Hz) by leveraging rolling shutter artifacts and an LED Gray-code counter.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: introduces the Density-weighted Volumetric Evaluation (DVE) metric using Mantaflow simulations to assess 3D velocity fields directly, alongside image-level (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), depth consistency (RMSEdepth), and temporal video metrics (CGVQM).

Extensive real-world and synthetic experiments with diverse fuel sources (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper) and insightful ablation studies demonstrating the importance of flow initialization, synchronization, and alpha masking.
weaknesses: Quantitative validation relies primarily on temporal hold-out (every 8th frame) across the three camera viewpoints rather than an explicit spatially held-out camera view for cross-view novel view synthesis evaluation.

The constant linear velocity and finite-lifetime Gaussian motion model is relatively simple and may oversmooth or struggle with highly turbulent vortical structures, smoke-fire boundary interactions, and accelerations over longer intervals.

Heavy reliance on 2D pre-processing models (MEMFOF for optical flow and Depth-Anything-V2 for depth priors), which can be noisy or inconsistent in semi-transparent, highly luminous, or low-texture flame regions.
